stimulus.text:
Immigration to the United States (U.S. Bureau of the Census, Statistical Abstract of the United States)

| Period | Immigrants |
| 1861–1870 | 2,314,824 |
| 1871–1880 | 2,812,191 |
| 1881–1890 | 5,246,613 |
| 1891–1900 | 3,687,564 |

Figures are totals for each ten-year period.

In single years: 1882 saw 788,992 immigrants arrive, and 1890 saw 455,302.
stimulus.source_note: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Statistical Abstract of the United States (1943), Table 107. Public data.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Statistical Abstract of the United States (1943), Table 107

stem: The table shows immigration nearly doubling between 1871–1880 and 1881–1890. That jump lines up best with which change described in the books?

options.text: The arrival of “new immigrants” from southern and eastern Europe
The end of all immigration from Ireland and Germany
options.misconception: Ends an immigration flow that continued.
Closes a station that opened later and received immigrants.

options.text: The repeal of the Chinese Exclusion Act
options.misconception: Repeals a law that was actually renewed.

rationales.A: The books say the 1880s brought the new wave from southern and eastern Europe, which drove the decade’s surge.
rationales.B: Irish and German immigration continued. It was joined by new groups, not ended.
rationales.C: Ellis Island opened in 1892, after the 1880s surge, and it received immigrants rather than closing.
rationales.D: The Exclusion Act was never repealed in this period. It was renewed and made permanent in 1902.
rationales.general:
Match the surge to the wave the books describe.
1. The 1880s total nearly doubles the 1870s total.
2. The books say the 1880s brought the new wave from southern and eastern Europe.
3. That wave is the change that fits the timing and the size.
4. Irish and German immigration went on, and Ellis Island came later.
Background: before 1880 most immigrants came from Ireland, Germany, and Britain.
Remember: match a jump in the numbers to the change that fits its timing.
